Article Title: Asian Games: Defending champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy, Chirag Shetty suffer shock first-round exit
Article Text:
India’s Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty (IANS image)

Satwik-Chirag surrender early advantage

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Setback after team event bronze

NEW DELHI: India suffered a major setback in badminton at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday as defending men's doubles champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty were knocked out in the opening round.The fourth-seeded Indian pair, who were among the country's leading medal hopes, were stunned by Thailand's Pakkapan Teeraratsakul and Peeratchai Sukphun, losing 21-12, 19-21, 14-21 in a contest that lasted one hour and eight minutes.The defeat ended Satwik and Chirag's bid to defend the gold medal they won at the previous edition of the Asian Games The Indian duo made an impressive start and appeared to be in control after taking the opening game 21-12 in 20 minutes.However, Teeraratsakul and Sukphun gradually found their rhythm and turned the contest around. The Thai pair kept the pressure on the Indians in the second game and eventually edged it 21-19 after 24 minutes to force a decider.Satwik and Chirag were unable to regain their momentum in the final game. The Thai pair quickly took control and completed the upset in just 19 minutes, winning the decider 21-14.The Indian pair's inability to close out the match after winning the opening game proved costly as the Thai shuttlers produced a composed finish to seal one of the major upsets of the badminton competition.The early exit is a disappointing start to India's individual badminton campaign after the men's team secured a bronze medal in the team competition.Satwik and Chirag had entered the men's doubles draw as the fourth seeds and were expected to challenge for another podium finish after their gold-medal success at the previous Asian Games at Hangzhou.Instead, their campaign ended in the first round, leaving India without one of its biggest medal contenders in the men's doubles event.
Article Summary: Defending men's doubles champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty knocked out in the opening round. The fourth-seeded Indian pair were stunned by Thailand's Pakkapan Teeraratsakul and Peeratchai Sukphun, losing 21-12, 19-21, 14-21.

Article Title: '15 years ... I waited for long': Krishna Jaisankar set for her India moment at Asian Games
Article Text:
Krishna Jaisankar (Image credit: Agencies)

A long road to the India jersey

Paris 2024 became a turning point

From a basketball family to shot put

Chasing Asian Games glory

Olympics - the ultimate dream

The chase for 18 metres

'Dreams do come true'

Whenever Krishna Jaisankar gets some time, she opens her kit bag and looks at the badge on her T-shirt.It has one word written on it: INDIA.Every time she looks at it, her eyes get moist. But there is also a sense of confidence that builds within her. After waiting for 15 years, Krishna knows that when she finally wears the India jersey in Japan, it will mean much more than simply making her Asian Games debut.For the 23-year-old shot putter, the jersey will represent 15 years of ups and downs, missed opportunities, injuries and countless moments when she had to pick herself up and start again.“It's a surreal feeling. I just can't wait to don that jersey in Japan. 15 years.... I waited for long and yes, I have earned it. I am very appreciative, like I'm very grateful for the opportunity and to be able to finally put Team India on my back,” Krishna told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.After missing out on selection several times, Krishna finally broke through and earned her place in the Indian team for the Asian Games 2026.Now, as she prepares to travel to Japan, the Indian shot putter wants to leave the old disappointments behind and write a new chapter - one that she hopes will end with a medal.Her message to herself when she reaches Japan is simple.“All right, it's showtime,” Krishna said.Krishna's journey has never been an easy one. There were moments when she wanted to give up. She left India at a young age, first moving to Jamaica and later to the United States, as she looked for opportunities to develop as an athlete.Then came the Commonwealth Games opportunity. Krishna was among the favourites to make it to the big event, but a hamstring injury disrupted her plans.She tore her hamstring just three weeks before the event. Yet, she returned to competition and managed to qualify for the Asian Games. She also became the national champion after 15 years.“I just think the fighter mentality that I have. Never to give up. Never to settle. Setbacks are meant for something. Setbacks are supposed to mould you, but not define you,” she said.The biggest setback came in 2024. Marred by injuries, Krishna missed the Paris Olympics. But the difficult phase also forced her to look closely at herself and rethink the way she was approaching her career.She began paying more attention to her nutrition, sleep and recovery. She also started spending more time reflecting and talking to herself.“It was a very rough period for me,” she said.“I left my country, left my family, left my comfort zone. What does my opportunity cost? What am I getting back? I'm not making the team, I'm not competing. Why am I getting injured?” she said.That period eventually changed her approach towards her ultimate goal - representing India.Instead of looking too far ahead, Krishna decided to take things one step at a time.“If you've got a dream, you've got to protect it. You have a dream, you've got to protect it,” Krishna said.Krishna grew up in a sporting family. Her parents, Prasanna and Jay Shankar, have been involved in basketball, and she closely watched the work they put into developing the sport. Her mother has also been a national selector for Indian basketball.But Krishna eventually chose athletics and found her own identity in shot put.“I think my inspiration was within my corners, which is my family. Whatever I am today it is because of their support. I wanted to choose a different sport and I did and I am really happy about it,” she said.“Thanks to the Reliance Foundation, the Athletics Federation of India, the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu, and everyone in Tamil Nadu. Everybody has supported me and believed in me,” the 23-year-old said.Making her Team India debut at the Asian Games is a special moment for Krishna. But she does not want the excitement of finally making the team to overshadow her bigger target - winning a medal.Once she is in Japan, she wants to treat the competition like any other championship.“Now it's go time, there is no look back. I am looking forward, looking ahead in the future,” she said.“It's going to be a show, man. It's going to be a show from all sectors of athletics. Let it be track, let it be field, we're going to put up a show. All we ask in return, support us. Keep us in your prayers,” Krishan said.For Krishna, the Asian Games is not the end goal. It is a start. Her bigger dream is the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.She carries an Olympic chain with her even though she is yet to compete at the Games. For her, it is a reminder of where she wants to go.“I'm not an Olympian, but every single day I aspire to be one. I'm confident now I can say that that dream is no longer a dream. It's like, I'm converting it to be a reality,” she said.Krishna won a gold medal at the National Federation Cup 2026 and, in the process, broke her own record of 17.09m. She won the top prize with a personal best throw of 17.35m.Now, Krishna has set herself the target of crossing 18 metres. She believes the Asian Games 2026 will be a great platform to achieve that feat while also challenging for the gold medal.“I am getting closer,” she said. “But again, it's very important to believe in the process. No better place to do it than Japan. Let's have a PB in Japan. I know I am a medal contender,” she said. “So, the mindset also is walking into the thing and be like, you know what, I'm walking in as a medal contender, not as a participant,” she said.Bodyshaming: Turning comments into strengthKrishna has been muscular since childhood. Her appearance sometimes made her uncomfortable. She felt that she did not fit what she believed was society's traditional idea of how a woman should look.“I didn't even know the meaning of body shaming until, you know, somebody came and told me, hey, somebody's body shaming you,” she said.But over the years, Krishna learned to see her body differently. The same body that some people made fun of became the body that helped her break records and earn her place in Team India.“To show the world, to show the society, that the body that you're making fun of and making me feel that I'm ashamed of is the body that's helping me break records, is the body that's helping me debut for Team India at the Asian Games,” she said.Her message to young girls is direct.“Be confident in who you are. Do not change yourself for somebody. She also has another message: do not live for other people's approval. Do not seek validation from people because again, comparison is a thief of joy,” she said.With 15 years of pain now behind her, Krishna is ready to write a new chapter in Japan. When she steps into the throwing circle with the shot in her hand, the 23-year-old will perhaps remember the 18-year-old version of herself who first dared to dream of representing India.Asked what she would say to the 18-year-old Krishna, the 23-year-old replied: “Dreams do come true”.“Know that your story is not just your journey. It's a story of so many untold stories. There are so many people that look up to you. If you have a dream, you bloody protect it,” Krishna signed off.
Article Summary: Krishna Jaisankar will make her Asian Games debut at the 2026 Games. The 23-year-old shot putter has waited 15 years for recognition. She has overcome injuries and missed opportunities to make the team. Krishna grew up in a sporting family and is the daughter of a basketball player.

Article Title: Asian Games: Joshna Chinappa makes history with sixth medal; Anahat, Abhay storm into semis as India assure three squash medals
Article Text:
Anahat Singh and Joshna Chinappa (PTI/ANI Photos)

Joshna seals sixth Asian Games medal

Anahat, Abhay march into singles semifinals

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India assured themselves of three squash medals at the Asian Games 2026 on Friday as Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar entered the mixed doubles semifinals, while Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh advanced to the last four in the women’s and men’s singles respectively.For Joshna, the semifinal berth carried added significance. The 40-year-old, competing at her record seventh Asian Games, secured her sixth medal at the continental showpiece with Senthilkumar. The Indian duo produced a dominant 11-3, 11-5 win over the Philippines’ David Pelino and Jemyca Aribado in their quarterfinal.Junior world champion Anahat and Abhay also continued their campaigns with straight-game victories, leaving India with three medal assurances across the squash events.Joshna and Senthilkumar needed less than half an hour to dispatch the Philippine pair at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena. The Indians took control from the start, racing to a 3-0 lead and quickly extending it to 9-2 before wrapping up the opening game 11-3 in nine minutes.The second game was more competitive initially, with Pelino and Aribado reducing the deficit to 4-2. But Joshna and Senthilkumar shifted gears again, moving to 7-2 and then 8-4 before closing out the match 11-5.They will face Hong Kong’s Yo Ka Lee and Ming Hong Tang in Saturday’s semifinal.“Winning a medal for your country is always very special. And that's been my motivation all my career,” Joshna told PTI after the match.The medal will take Joshna’s Asian Games tally to six, including two silver. Her previous medals include a singles bronze in 2018, team silver in 2014 and 2018, and team bronze in 2010 and 2022.Joshna has now surpassed Saurav Ghosal’s record of six Asian Games appearances, having competed at every edition since the 2002 Busan Games.Anahat continued her impressive campaign with a commanding 11-2, 11-5, 11-3 victory over compatriot Tanvi Khanna in the women’s singles quarterfinal.The junior world champion and medal favourite will now look to take another step towards the gold medal and a potential Olympic qualification. The singles gold medallists at the Asian Games will directly qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its Olympic debut.In the men’s singles, Abhay overcame local favourite Ryonosuke Tsukue 11-4, 11-3, 11-6 to book his place in the last four.He will face Pakistan’s Irfan Muhammad, who defeated India’s Veer Chotrani 6-11, 11-8, 11-3, 11-3 in 41 minutes after recovering from a game down.
Article Summary: India secure three squash medals at the Asian Games 2026. Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar into mixed doubles semifinals. Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh advance to last four in women's and men's singles.

Article Title: Her mother thought she was in Bengaluru. Seema Kumari was actually winning Asian Games bronze in Nagoya
Article Text:
Seema (Image credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

On Thursday night, when a beaming Seema Kumari took a short lap of honour draped in the tricolour, congratulatory messages began pouring in. It was perhaps then that her mother realised her daughter was in Nagoya and not Bengaluru.Seema’s 75-year-old mother, who lives in Reta in Himachal Pradesh, suffers from hypertension. Concerned about her daughter’s well-being, she is often kept in the dark about Seema’s travels and competitions.But after the stupendous performance Seema delivered on a windy night at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, her mother will have plenty to celebrate. So will a nation, after the 25-year-old opened India’s athletics medal account with a bronze in the women’s 10,000m.In a tight race, Seema clocked 32:50.05 to finish behind Bahrain’s Winfred Yavi (32:39.18) and Japan’s Nozomi Tanaka (32:41.54).Her bronze ended India’s 16-year wait for a medal in the event at the Asian Games. Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut had won gold and silver respectively, at the 2010 Games.It was a race built on endurance, pace, persistence and planning. Up against a star-studded field, Seema could have been forgiven for feeling the pressure.Instead, she focused on the distance rather than the runners around her.Her consistency was remarkable. Across all 25 laps, she never fell out of the leading pack. With two laps to go, she even raised hopes of a silver, but Bahrain’s Yavi stepped on the gas at the 200m mark and Tanaka accelerated, leaving Seema to settle for bronze.For Seema, who lost her father at a young age and is one of six siblings, it was a special medal on her Asian Games debut.“The race was very tactical. Everyone ran for the medal and I also thought that I would fight for it. Although I’m happy that I’ve earned a medal in my first Asian Games, I hope to change the colour of the medal in the 5000 metres event.”The past year-and-a-half has seen Seema on a rising curve training under coach Scott Simmons.“I’ve been training with Simmons for the past three years and have been sent to the USA for camps and training. It is very beneficial because conditions are tough there and we train with Olympic champions,” she said. Seema won a silver at the World University Games last year.As expected, India’s medal of the day came from the 4x400m mixed relay team. In a thrilling comeback, the quartet of Manu Saji, MR Poovamma, Vishal TK and Vithya Ramraj clocked 3:14.46 to take silver behind Bahrain, who won gold in a Games-record timing of 3:12.87.India did not have the best of starts, with Manu unable to provide the initial momentum. Poovamma, however, hauled the team back into contention with a strong second leg.Vishal then closed the gap and put India firmly in medal bracket before Vithya produced an impressive anchor leg. With the Vietnam runner breathing down her neck, she held her nerve in the home straight to fend off the challenge. The Vietnamese quartet finished just 0.08 seconds behind with 3:14.54.Jay Kumar and Kiran Phal, who ran the morning heats, were replaced with Vishal and Vithya for the final.Asha Ilango narrowly missed out on a triple jump medal, finishing fourth behind China’s Li Yi on countback after both athletes recorded a best jump of 13.83m. Asha needed to better 13.79m with her final attempt to move ahead of Li, but could manage only 13.59m. The other Indian in the fray, Niharika Vashisht, finished 10th.Gurindervir Singh eased into the 100m semifinals. He clocked 10.38 seconds to finish second in Heat 4. Animesh Kujur also qualified for the 100m semifinals.
Article Summary: Seema Kumari won bronze in the women's 10,000m. Her bronze ended India’s 16-year wait for a medal in the event at the Asian Games. The 25-year-old won a silver at the World University Games last year.

Article Title: 'We didn’t eat, drink or sleep': Rowers Satnam and Salman recall turmoil before historic Asian Games bronze
Article Text:
Satnam-Salman win rowing bronze

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: Earlier this week, Typhoon Dujuan disrupted the Asian Games schedule and triggered a storm of a different kind in Indian rowing.A contingent that won five medals at the previous edition in Hangzhou will return home with just one — a bronze won by Satnam Singh and Salman Khan in the men’s double sculls.The duo had originally been entered in the quadruple sculls before being moved to the doubles following 11th-hour changes by the Rowing Federation of India (RFI), which attributed the reshuffle to the curtailed competition schedule.At the Nagaragawa International Regatta Course in Gifu Prefecture on Thursday, Satnam and Salman stayed in the leading pack for much of the race. China’s Xudi Yi and Yide Nie eventually pulled away to win gold in 6:09.77, ahead of Uzbekistan’s Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov and Pavel Sorin (6:10.49). The Indian pair finished in 6:13.25.The medal dulled the bitterness of the previous few days, but did little to erase it.“The hardest part was that we were removed from the quadruple and placed into the doubles. We were depressed. We didn’t eat or drink or sleep that night. We were harassed and had no recovery,” Salman said.With a medal at stake, a first for India in the Asian Games men’s double sculls, the rowers had to put the upheaval aside.“The next day, we woke up and felt that what matters most is the country and the flag. We have to keep it high. Whatever happens later will happen. We want to make sure that whatever happened to us shouldn’t happen to any other rower,” Salman said.“We had a chance to raise the flag of our country high but we lost it. Koi nahi. Jo kismat mein hota wahi milta hai. If it is in our destiny to win something, then it is impossible to stop it,” he added.Satnam, though, could not help wondering what might have been.“The situation we faced two days before was very unexpected. If we had been formed four months ago, then we could have been fighting for gold,” said the Navy rower. “But I am feeling proud since we have never won a medal in double sculls. I feel sad for my partners (from the quadruple sculls) because a good medal has gone from our hands.”Upset by the changes before the race, Salman recalled the advice his coaches gave him before the race: “Salman, aisa chappu maro ki nadi ka paani bahar aa jaye. (Row your oars with such force that the water overflows from the river.)”The line brought a smile to his face. “You get so motivated with such words that you can row with a stone as well,” he said.
Article Summary: India's Satnam Singh and Salman Khan win bronze in the men's double sculls. Pair had originally been entered in the quadruple before being moved to the doubles. China's Xudi Yi and Yide Nie eventually pulled away to win gold in 6:09.77.

Article Title: Asian Games: Diya Chitale, Manush Shah storm into mixed doubles semifinals, assure table tennis medal
Article Text:
Diya Chitale and Manush Shah (Image credit: X)

Strong finish seals the win

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's fourth table tennis medal

NEW DELHI: India's Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a medal in the mixed doubles event at the Asian Games after pulling off a big win over Hong Kong's Wong Chun-Ting and Doo Hoi Kem in the quarterfinals on Friday.The Indian pair beat the world No. 4 combination 3-1 (11-6, 13-15, 11-9, 11-5) to enter the semifinals and assure India of a table tennis medal.Manush and Diya will now face China's world No. 2 pair Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha in the semifinals later on Friday. A win would take the Indians into the final of an Asian Games table tennis event for the first time.The medal is India's second in mixed doubles at the Asian Games. Sharath Kamal and Manika Batra had won bronze in Jakarta in 2018. It is also only India's fourth table tennis medal in the history of the Asian Games.Manush and Diya made an excellent start, taking the opening game 11-6. The Hong Kong pair fought back in the second game, but the Indians stayed in the contest before narrowly losing it 13-15.With the match level at 1-1, the Indian duo raised their game and took the third game 11-9. That put them just one game away from a guaranteed medal.They completed the job in style, racing to an 11-5 win in the fourth game to seal their place in the last four.India have now won four table tennis medals at the Asian Games, with all four being bronze.Sharath Kamal and Manika Batra won the mixed doubles bronze at Jakarta 2018. The men's team also claimed bronze at the same Games, with Harmeet Desai, G Sathiyan and Manav Thakkar part of that squad.At Hangzhou 2023, Sutirtha Mukherjee and Ayhika Mukherjee added another bronze in women's doubles.
Article Summary: India's Manush Shah and Diya Chitale beat Hong Kong's Wong Chun-Ting and Doo Hoi Kem 3-1 in the quarterfinals of the mixed doubles event at the Asian Games. It is India's fourth table tennis medal in the history of the Games. They will face China's Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha in the semifinals later on Friday.

Article Title: Two-time Olympic champion Shaunae Miller-Uibo named VDHM International Event Ambassador
Article Text:
Two-time Olympic champion Shaunae Miller-Uibo announced as International Event Ambassador for Delhi Half Marathon 2026

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Two-time Olympic 400m champion Shaunae Miller-Uibo has been named the International Event Ambassador for the Vedanta Delhi Half Marathon (VDHM), promoted by Procam International. The 21st edition of the prestigious road race will be held on Oct 18 at the Jawaharlal Nehru stadium here.The Bahamian sprinting star is among the most accomplished athletes of her generation. She created history by winning Olympic gold in the women’s 400m at both the Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Games. Her successful title defence in Tokyo made her only the second woman, after France’s Marie-José Perec, to win consecutive Olympic 400m titles. Her winning time of 48.36 seconds remains a North American record.Miller-Uibo has enjoyed sustained success at the World Athletics Championships. After winning silver medals in the 400m in 2015 and 2019 and a bronze in the 200m in 2017, she finally claimed the 400m world title in Eugene in 2022. Her 200m personal best of 21.74 seconds is also a Bahamian national record. She has additionally won Commonwealth Games gold in the 200m and a mixed 4x400m relay gold for The Bahamas at the World Athletics Relays.Reflecting on her upcoming India visit, Miller-Uibo said she was excited to experience New Delhi and participate in a race with a strong connection to its community. She said the marathon brings together people from different backgrounds and abilities through the shared joy of running.“Progress is built one step at a time,” Miller-Uibo said, adding that she hoped her journey would encourage runners to trust their process, remain consistent and believe in what they can achieve.Beyond athletics, Miller-Uibo has been involved in charitable and community initiatives in The Bahamas, particularly those supporting children and young people.Procam International Joint Managing Director Vivek Singh said Miller-Uibo’s career demonstrated patience and persistence. He noted that her journey to the 2022 world title reflected the message of perseverance that the event hopes participants will carry on race day.
Article Summary: Two-time Olympic 400m champion Shaunae Miller-Uibo named International Event Ambassador for Vedanta Delhi Half Marathon 2026. The 21st edition of the prestigious road race will be held on Oct 18 at the Jawaharlal Nehru stadium here. She created history by winning Olympic gold in the women’s 400m at both the Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Games.

Article Title: Juggling Chess Olympiad prep and a commentary gig in India: The other side of USA's only female GM Irina Krush
Article Text:
The other side of America's only grandmaster Irina Krush

A little girl from Soviet Ukraine

A younger Irina Krush (Photo by Zeljka Malobabic)

You don’t want to look like the fool on the team with Magnus. GM Irina Krush

The cost of commentary

GM Irina Krush's prep before commentating on a game (Photo by Jyotirmoy Halder for TimesofIndia.com)

Eyes on Olympiad

Irina Krush (Photo by Photo by Lennart Ootes)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Any secret sauce?

NEW DELHI: For most of its history, American women’s chess had a very simple relationship with the Olympiad podium. It did not have one. Not once, in over four decades of trying, had the United States women’s team finished among the medals at chess’s biennial team championship.Then, in 2002, Susan Polgar switched her allegiance from Hungary to the United States. Two years later, after stepping away from top-level competition to raise her two sons, she sat down on Board 1 in Calvià, Mallorca, and dragged a young, unheralded American team to silver, second only to China and ahead of a Russian juggernaut that had ruled women’s chess for a generation.It was the first medal of any colour the country had ever won in the women’s category.Bronze followed in Dresden four years later, in 2008. And then, after a wait of 16 years that swallowed many careers, bronze again, this time in Budapest, at a tournament where India finally broke through for gold. Three medals across two decades somehow represented three different eras of American chess.The one name, however, that appears on the scoresheet every single time is that of Irina Krush, the first, and to this day the only, woman to earn the Grandmaster (GM) title while playing for the United States.“I was sort of the main player of my generation,” Krush, who is currently playing in her record-extending 13th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, said with a small, knowing smile during an exclusive interaction with TimesofIndia.com.The story does not begin in America. Krush was born in Odesa, in what was then Soviet Ukraine, and arrived in Brooklyn with her parents when she was five years old. Her father, an amateur player of real quality, taught her the moves.Her first tournament against adults followed when she was six, at the Manhattan Chess Club. She made her first appearance for the United States at the World Youth Championship in Poland at seven. By 11, she was already competing in the US Women’s Championship.At 14, in 1998, she won it. Still, almost three decades on, she remains the youngest champion in the event’s history.Krush’s association with India is a long one too. She fondly recalls playing against a young chess prodigy, Koneru Humpy. In the last few years, her association with India has also included a new part of her profession in chess broadcasting and commentary at the Global Chess League (GCL), a league she participated in during its inaugural 2023 season in Dubai, on a roster built around Magnus Carlsen.“It was a chance to play in the same team as Magnus, and it was like a very special opportunity,” Krush added. “I definitely thought that was like a highlight of my chess career.”But a highlight, in her telling, was never the same thing as a comfortable one. “It’s also — you feel the pressure, right? Because you don’t want to look like the fool on the team with Magnus,” she chuckled. “There are two sides to that coin. But overall, it was a very good experience.”She has not played in the league since. What she has done, for the next two seasons, is commentate on it, first in Mumbai and, more recently, in Bengaluru, watching from the other side of the glass.This time, Krush arrived in India with the 46th Chess Olympiad bearing down on her. For more than two decades, the tournament has been the anchor of her competitive identity, and this year, the games in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, were set to begin just two days after her India schedule wrapped up.The commentary booth, for all it has given her, though, has eaten directly into the time she would otherwise have spent getting ready for it.Asked plainly whether she had found any window to play or prepare between broadcasts, she replied: “So far, no. It’s only been a few days, but it’s been so busy. Today, we were asked to appear at the golf thing. So I had to get up at 7:45 in the morning, go to that. Then I had another nap, and then I just had to go here. So it’s a long day. And honestly, I have not had a chance to do much chess for myself at all.”It is a trade she has made with her eyes open, not a complaint dressed up as one. She had spent the months before India trying to bank the form the broadcast schedule was about to interrupt.“I’ve spent the summer playing tournaments, and I just finished a tournament the day before I came here,” she told this website. “There’s definitely been an attempt to try to get myself into good playing condition.”And on the final day, when the commentators were felicitated on the main stage for being the voice of the league, Krush, who became a grandmaster in 2013, barely lingered after the ceremony. She left the arena almost immediately, the next challenge, the Samarkand Olympiad, already waiting.For someone who has spent much of her career playing chess at the highest level, commentary came without formal preparation.“I never did anything special. I don’t have any training in commentary,” she said. “But, you know, it comes kind of naturally for me to talk about chess. It’s something that’s very easy to talk about and get excited about. I like to watch chess.”Her preparation for the booth is less about learning how to commentate and more about doing what she has always done with chess: looking closely at the players and their games.“You definitely try to do some preparation,” she said. “So, you have ways to fill up, you know, give some context for what’s happening. How are the players doing? So, it just requires a little bit of research, you know, to come up with those nuggets that people will find interesting.”But even that preparation changes as a tournament begins to take shape. “At the beginning, you’re doing more general research,” she further noted. “And after the players have started playing against each other, then you’re already more interested in what’s happening in this tournament. What’s the recent results? Not like what happened one year ago in their other matchups.”“As the tournament continues, you start focussing more. What happened in the first half? How do they do again? How are they overall doing in the tournament?” Krush continued.“The tournament itself becomes more of a focus than their history before. Because it’s all now about, like, now you’ve already seen their recent form. So, you focus more on that. Looking at the games is the best part.”The difficulty comes when the chess stops. “The only challenge is, like, maybe sometimes you gotta fill up the time,” she admitted. “You know, the games are over. For me, it’s like, okay, just commenting on the things that are not as exciting for me. You know, just figuring out what to say.“But when we’re on the chess, it’s the easiest.”The United States are among the leading teams at the Women’s Chess Olympiad, with a squad featuring Carissa Yip, Alice Lee, Rose Atwell and Tatev Abrahamyan, alongside the most experienced Irina Krush.“It’s like a very nice mix of the young players who are really kind of, they’re not even at their peak yet necessarily, but they’re definitely rising,” Krush said. “And then, okay, like there’s me and Tatev, and we kind of bring a lot of experience to the team. Playing for like 20 years or more for the Olympiad.”That depth, the 42-year-old says, is the product of a sport that barely resembles the one she came up in.“It’s much more competitive (now). There’s more incentive to play chess, more opportunities to play,” the eight-time US women’s champion shared. “We didn’t have the kinds of prizes we have at the US championships 25 years ago. We didn’t have an American Cup. We didn’t have a Cairns Cup. We didn’t have the Cairns Queen chess award for the next woman who’s gonna become a grandmaster in America.”The dividend, she adds, is visible in the players coming up behind her now.“A whole generation of strong girls coming up, with Carissa and Alice being kind of the main ones, but also other young girls who are close to 2400 as well,” Krush acknowledged.In Uzbekistan, the US women’s team made a dream start, but its campaign soon lost momentum. A draw against Uzbekistan was followed by a defeat to India, leaving Krush’s team in 14th place in the rankings heading into the rest day.For someone who has now spent two seasons narrating other people’s games for a living, Krush is unsentimental about what the job actually requires.Asked what advice she would give someone hoping to follow her into a commentary booth, she does not reach for a formula.ALSO READ: From uplifting heartbroken team to calling out Chess Olympiad hotel mess: Srinath is India's man to count on “Honestly, there’s just a lot of people who are doing it these days, and everyone brings their own special thing to it, right? So you have different styles. You could be like a top GM and then just start doing commentary. You could be like a different level enthusiast and do commentary,” she concluded, while instinctively running her tongue once again along the outside of her gum. “So I really don’t have any advice except I feel like anyone who loves chess and is pretty good at it can do it. ”
Article Summary: Irina Krush is the only woman to earn the Grandmaster title while playing for the United States. She is currently playing in her record-extending 13th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Krush was born in Odesa, in what was then Soviet Ukraine, and arrived in Brooklyn with her parents when she was five.

Article Title: Asian Games: Aishwary Pratap Singh finishes fifth, Niraj Kumar eighth as India miss 50m rifle 3P individual medal after team silver
Article Text:
Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar (ANI Photo)

Aishwary and Niraj fail to convert qualification form into medals

India’s shooting tally reaches 10 medals

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s shooters missed out on a medal in the men’s 50m rifle 3 positions individual event at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday, despite securing silver in the team competition earlier in the day. Asian record holder Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar finished fifth in the individual final, while Niraj Kumar came last among the eight finalists, bringing a disappointing end to India’s campaign in the event.Aishwary, who had qualified third for the final, managed 327.6 points to finish fifth. Niraj, who had entered the final in fourth place in qualification, could only score 299 points to finish eighth.China’s Liu Yukun claimed gold with 360.5 points, setting a new Asian Games record. His compatriot Zhang Changhong took silver with 360.2 points, while Kazakhstan’s Islam Satpayev secured bronze with 348.3 points.The result was a setback for India after both shooters had shown promise in the qualification round. Aishwary, the Asian record holder, had finished third, while Niraj secured the fourth qualifying spot. However, neither could maintain that position in the final as China swept the top two places.The individual event disappointment followed India’s silver-medal finish in the men’s 50m rifle 3 positions team competition. Aishwary, Niraj and Rudrankksh Patil combined for a score of 1762-94x, finishing just behind China, who secured gold with 1766-95x. South Korea took bronze with 1751-87x.Aishwary scored 589-34x to finish third in the team qualification standings, while Niraj recorded 588-34x to place fourth. Rudrankksh, with 585-26x, finished ninth and missed out on a place in the individual final.India had won gold in the team event at the 2022 Asian Games but surrendered their title to China in Aichi-Nagoya.India’s shooting contingent has now collected 10 medals at the 2026 Asian Games, including one gold, five silver and four bronze medals. The only shooting gold so far came on Friday, when Suruchi and Kamaljeet won the 10m mixed air pistol event.The Indian pair defeated South Korea 484.6 to 478.0 in the final, with Iran taking bronze on 415.8 points. India’s winning score also broke the Asian record of 481.3, previously set by Uzbekistan at the Asian Shooting Championships in New Delhi earlier this year.India’s overall medal tally at the Games stood at 19 on Friday, comprising two gold, eight silver and nine bronze medals. The women’s cricket team had earlier secured India’s other gold, defeating Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final.The rifle team silver added to India’s medal haul, but the failure to convert two strong qualification performances into an individual podium finish left the shooters without another medal in the event.
Article Summary: India's shooting contingent has now collected 10 medals at the 2026 Asian Games. Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar finished fifth in the individual final, while Niraj Kumar came last among the eight finalists. India’s overall medal tally at the Games stood at 19, comprising two gold, eight silver and nine bronze medals.

Article Title: Nepal pull off stunning upset, beat Afghanistan by five wickets in Asian Games 2026
Article Text:
Nepal stun Afghanistan in Asian Games 2026 (Image: X)

Rohit, Sundeep rescue Nepal before captain finishes job

Afghanistan's batting collapses under spin pressure

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Afghanistan top Group A despite defeat

Nepal sent a warning to the rest of the competition with a stunning five-wicket upset over Afghanistan, chasing down 103 with 14 balls to spare in their Asian Games Group A opener at Korogi Sports Park on Friday. After their spinners strangled Afghanistan for just 102, Nepal recovered from a precarious 31/3 to complete a composed chase. Rohit Paudel, Sundeep Jora and captain Dipendra Singh Airee held their nerve to seal a memorable win.Nepal's chase got off to a disastrous start as they lost both openers cheaply. Afghanistan left-arm seamer Faridoon Dawoodzai dismissed Kushal Bhurtel for a duck before right-arm pacer Abdullah Ahmadzai removed Aasif Sheikh for two.Things got worse when Kushal Malla was run out in the seventh over, leaving Nepal struggling at 31/3 after 6.3 overs.Sundeep and Rohit then steadied the innings with a crucial partnership. The pair kept rotating the strike and punished loose deliveries to keep Nepal's chase alive. Sundeep smashed a four and a six across the ninth and 10th overs before being run out in the 10th, giving Afghanistan renewed hope.Rohit, however, remained composed and found a reliable partner in Dipendra.The duo avoided unnecessary risks, picking up singles and twos as Nepal moved steadily towards the target.With victory within touching distance, Rohit accelerated and hit three fours across the 16th and 17th overs. Dipendra fell in the 18th over with Nepal level with Afghanistan's total, but Gulsan Jha calmly collected a single to complete the chase.Rohit finished unbeaten on 33 off 32 balls, while Sundeep made 34 off 35 and Dipendra contributed 15 off 18.Earlier, Nepal's spinners had put Afghanistan under pressure from the outset. Kushal Bhurtel and Lalit Rajbanshi shared seven wickets between them, preventing Afghanistan's batters from building significant partnerships.Rajbanshi was particularly economical, finishing with three wickets for just 13 runs from his four overs, while Bhurtel claimed four wickets as Afghanistan struggled to score freely. Faisal Shinozada and Najibullah Zadran were Afghanistan's top scorers, both making 30, while Nangeyalia Kharoti contributed 17.But with the rest of the batting lineup unable to accelerate, Afghanistan were restricted to 102.The defeat leaves Afghanistan with one win and one loss from their two Group A matches. Despite the setback, they remain at the top of the three-team table on net run rate, having completed their league campaign.Nepal, meanwhile, have made the perfect start and will face winless Japan in their final group game. With each team playing two league matches, the top two sides from each group will advance to the quarter-finals.
Article Summary: Rohit Paudel, Sundeep Jora and captain Dipendra Singh Airee held their nerve to seal a memorable win. Nepal recovered from a precarious 31/3 to complete a composed chase. Afghanistan remain at the top of the three-team table on net run rate, having completed their league campaign.

Article Title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi to replace Tilak Varma or Shivam Dube in ‘six months’, predicts ex-India cricketer
Article Text:
Tilak Varma, Ishan Kishan, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What type of batter do you prefer in the T20I setup? Aggressive boundary-hitter Adaptable innings constructor 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Mohammad Kaif believes India could face a major selection headache in the T20I format within the next six months, with the former batter predicting that Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will force his way into the first-choice side.Kaif feels the teenage sensation’s emergence could eventually leave either Tilak Varma or Shivam Dube fighting for a place in the playing XI, despite Tilak currently being India’s vice-captain.“I understand that Tilak is the vice-captain. But vice-captains have also been dropped before. I do not want to go there. Shivam Dube is not scoring in every game and still has to prove himself. Fielding is also his weakness, and he is not a proper bowling all-rounder. He is only playing as a batter. After six months, either Tilak or Dube will be out. You will have to remove one, and Sooryavanshi will play. I am saying this right now", Kaif said on his YouTube channel.Kaif pointed to Sooryavanshi’s performances beyond T20Is as another reason for his prediction. The teenager also made an impact in the Duleep Trophy and even bowled during the tournament, adding another dimension to his game.“Sooryavanshi scored in the Duleep Trophy as well. He has improved his game. He was even bowling there. So he has understood that if he can bowl a few overs, he will have an advantage,” he added.The numbers behind Sooryavanshi’s rapid rise are difficult to overlook. In his first six T20Is of 2026, he has scored 193 runs at an average of 32.17 and a strike rate of 189.22. He has found the boundary once every 3.4 deliveries and hit a six every 7.2 balls.His IPL campaign strengthened that case further. Sooryavanshi finished the season with 776 runs at an average of 48.50 and a strike rate of 237.51, including 72 sixes.Those numbers have already shifted the conversation around the teenager. Rather than being viewed solely as a young player being gradually introduced to international cricket, Sooryavanshi is increasingly making a case for a regular place in India’s T20I setup.Tilak’s numbers, meanwhile, remain respectable on the surface. He has scored 395 runs in T20Is in 2026 at an average of 35.91 and a strike rate of 154.90.However, the timing of some of those runs adds another layer to the debate. His fifty came in the fifth and final T20I against England, by which point India had already lost the series, and India went on to lose that match as well.Another notable contribution came during the Zimbabwe tour, although the quality of the opposition bowling was not necessarily of the highest pedigree.There have also been occasions when Tilak has found it difficult to rotate the strike after being promoted up the order or arriving at the crease earlier than expected, particularly against spin. At the other end of the innings, however, he has shown greater effectiveness as a finisher, including against Jofra Archer.That creates a contrast in the type of batter India could eventually have to choose between. Sooryavanshi represents an extreme-tempo approach built around relentless boundary-hitting, while Tilak offers greater adaptability and the ability to construct an innings.Dube’s numbers also make the selection debate more complicated than Kaif’s assessment might suggest.The all-rounder has scored 415 T20I runs in 2026 at an average of 31.92 and a strike rate of 170.78. At the T20 World Cup, he scored 235 runs at a strike rate of 169.06, giving India substantial returns from a player primarily selected for his power-hitting.The more pertinent question surrounding Dube is his bowling contribution.He has bowled only 26 overs across 23 T20Is in 2026, taking 12 wickets while conceding 12.44 runs per over. Those figures underline how India have largely used him as a batter who can provide occasional overs rather than as a genuine bowling all-rounder.That distinction could become important if Sooryavanshi continues to add bowling to his skill set.For now, India have a number of options in their T20I batting group. But Kaif’s six-month prediction has put the spotlight firmly on a question that could become increasingly difficult for the selectors to avoid: how long can a player with Sooryavanshi’s scoring numbers remain outside the first-choice XI?
Article Summary: Sooryavanshi has scored 193 runs in his first six T20Is of 2026. He has found the boundary once every 3.4 deliveries and hit a six every 7.2 balls. The teenager also made an impact in the Duleep Trophy and even bowled during the tournament, adding another dimension to his game.

(Will you have tea or coffee?)," says Akash Deep while adjusting his chair in the hotel lobby. Second, he can't wait to check out of the hotel in Bengaluru, which has been his home for the past seven months.The 29-year-old has been included in the 15-member Rest of India squad, led by Rishabh Pant, which will take on 2025-26 Ranji Trophy champions Jammu and Kashmir in the Irani Cup match, starting from October 1 in Srinagar. The last time Akash Deep was in action was during the Ranji Trophy semifinal for Bengal, where they lost to the eventual champions, Jammu and Kashmir, by six wickets. It was during this match that Akash Deep suffered a lower-back stress fracture."I played that match with a 102 fever. It was my call and when it comes to playing for Bengal, I don't think twice. That state has given me so much. Whatever I am is because of Cricket Association Bengal (CAB).Even in the future, if I have to take a risk for Bengal to have a chance to win the Ranji Trophy, I will not think twice before taking it," says Akash.He smiles when asked about the risk of pushing himself at the end of the season, where he played every single game for the state across formats. The layoff turned out to be longer than he would have liked as it also ruled him out of the IPL 2026. Was it worth it?(For cricketers like us, we need to prove our credentials in every chance we get). It is easy to say, oh, I could have skipped that match... The workload was high, but it was a Ranji Trophy semifinal and there was a chance for us to lift that trophy. I know the injury gave a dent to my wallet as I missed out on the IPL, missed international cricket, but for me, I saw an opportunity where I had the chance to do something special on a bigger stage," he explains.The long layoff was frustrating but he chooses to focus on the brighter side and even during the difficult days, the opportunity to spend time with his family gave him happy memories. And the icing on the cake was sister's recovery from cancer."Spending weeks in the hotel rooms is not ideal. It is tough. But for me, these six months have been fruitful as well. My elder sister recovered from cancer. I got married, got appointed as Deputy Superintendent of Police by the Bihar government and, most importantly, got married," he laughs.Behind all the giggles, laughter and excitement of making a comeback lies a painful chapter in Akash's life. He has endured rejection, contemplated quitting cricket, lost his father and elder brother, searched for an oxygen cylinder for his mother during the Covid-19 pandemic and even learned to drive a truck to make ends meet.Yet, when he speaks about the darkest phase of his life, it is none of these moments that he recalls. His sister Akhand Jyoti Singh's cancer diagnosis broke him."She was the one who had forced me to pursue cricket. There was a time I thought of quitting cricket. She kept me going and when she was diagnosed with cancer, I was shattered. I was pleading with God, please not her. I have lost my father, my brother, how much more will God take from me? What would I do with all the money and fame if I won't have people to enjoy those with?" he says."Luckily, I was playing for Lucknow Super Giants (LSG) in the IPL. Every day, after completing the training, I used to rush to the hospital and come back around 2:30 am, and on the match day, I used to go to the hospital straight after the match and come back in the morning. I was not eating properly. I was not training properly. I had no focus on my cricket. Then there were travels in the IPL. I was scared that I might lose her," he adds.Post IPL, Akash Deep went to England, where his heroics at Edgbaston helped India win the Test. "She was going through chemotherapy. I was again all over the place. She told me to play for her and that's why I dedicated my match-winning performance to her," he recollects.Akash praises the BCCI 's Centre of Excellence (CoE) for helping him regain complete match fitness. The crafty seamer dismissed the criticism surrounding the CoE and its injury management."I am here for so many months now and I never faced any issue. There was a clear plan given to me and I have recovered following the instructions given by the CoE. It is a world-class facility. I have played cricket in other countries as well, but I must say when it comes to infrastructure, CoE is way ahead," he says.(Let me ask you something: if you have damaged your liver by drinking alcohol, is the doctor responsible for that?). We should have a CoE-like facility in every state of India," he adds.Fit again, Akash knows the road won't be easy for him. He will have to toil again to regain his place in the Indian team. There is pressure, but his body's readiness and the excitement to regain his spot give him the feeling of a kid in a candy shop."I will have to perform well in the Irani Trophy first. Then, if picked, I need to do well for India A. Yes, I want to make a comeback in the Indian team and it won't be that easy. But I am ready for the grind," he says.Over the years, Akash has navigated trials, tribulations, fame and accolades, his journey has been as unpredictable as the road he grew up near. He describes it in his own words: "" (My journey has been like the road in my village, topsy-turvy).He hails from Sasaram, a place steeped in history, where Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri defeated Mughal emperor Humayun at the Battle of Chausa in 1539. It was during Sher Shah Suri's reign that the Grand Trunk Road, also known as the Sher Shah Suri Road, was built. And perhaps there is something fitting about that: Akash Deep's journey, much like the GT Road that runs through India, has been rough, winding and uneven, but it has carried him a long way.
Article Summary: Akash Deep has been out of action for seven months owing to an injury. The 29-year-old has been included in the 15-member Rest of India squad, led by Rishabh Pant, which will take on 2025-26 Ranji Trophy champions Jammu and Kashmir in the Irani Cup match, starting from October 1.

Article Title: 'The night I could not sleep': Gautam Gambhir opens up on 'toughest decision' to drop Sanju Samson for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

India head coach Gautam Gambhir has revealed the emotional difficulty behind one of his biggest selection calls in T20Is, admitting that dropping Sanju Samson during the England series left him unable to sleep.Samson, who was named Player of the Tournament during India's T20 World Cup triumph earlier this year, was left out after the first match of the five-game series in England in July. India had lost that opening T20I, with teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi coming into the XI for his T20I debut in Manchester.Gambhir said the decision weighed heavily on him, particularly because Samson had played such an important role in India's World Cup success. Speaking to JioStar ahead of India's home season against the West Indies, the India coach revealed just how difficult the call was."In two years of my journey, that was the only night I could not sleep and I told this to Sanju because I knew that it was probably the toughest decision in my coaching tenure in a T20 format because someone who was player of the tournament, and then you have to leave him out after three or four games.And the reason was probably Vaibhav was in that kind of form as well, and we had to win the series.“Because ultimately you are there and when you are playing for India, or when you are coaching India, you want to win each and every series possible. I had a very, very honest conversation with him and I told him that that is one of the reasons why, because Vaibhav was in that kind of form, and we needed someone to score runs at the top, we needed that little bit of a platform at the top as well. And he was fine with it. And that's a conversation which me and Sanju had, and he took it in good spirits," said Gambhir.The call was eventually reversed when India returned home for their three-match T20I series against Afghanistan. Samson came back into the side at Sooryavanshi's expense and went on to hit back-to-back fifties as India completed a 3-0 series sweep.Gambhir also used the episode to explain why even a player in exceptional form cannot automatically expect a place in India's playing XI."I know, it is (tough). But then, I made him understand that I know you're in good form, but sometimes with the players who have done well for a long time, you will have to wait for your opportunity.“There’s one more thing - social media or outside noise doesn't decide the playing eleven. Playing eleven who, in that dressing room, or who the coach and captain feel can win us the match, or what is the best playing eleven, and who have done well for such a long time because if Vaibhav plays today, then it's going to be a tough conversation between me and whoever we leave out, whether it's Abhishek or Sanju.“So we can't suddenly ignore that a combination that has created such an impact over the last one and a half or two years, that after three or four failures we drop them and play a young player who is very talented, who is also in very good form.“So sometimes you will have to wait for your opportunity and we still want to create that security in that dressing room. Because it is very easy for me to take popular decisions, but it is probably the toughest thing for me to take the right decisions and we've taken the right decision of continuing with Sanju and Abhishek," he explained.Sooryavanshi's emergence has nevertheless added another dimension to India's T20I selection puzzle. The teenager made his international debut in Manchester, but Gambhir stressed that India's established combination cannot be discarded simply because a young player is performing well.For the India coach, maintaining continuity remains particularly important given the team's recent success. Gambhir pointed to the short turnaround between India's World Cup triumphs while arguing against overreacting to isolated setbacks."For two years, imagine, you imagine we won the World Cup - which team in the history of sport has gone undefeated from one World Cup to the other and gone on to win the World Cup?“It didn't take these guys 17 years to win the second World Cup. It took these guys only 17 months to win the third World Cup. Suddenly one bad series or three bad games here and there does not make them a bad player or does not make us a bad side. So it was very important for us to have that continuity."
Article Summary: Gautam Gambhir admits dropping Sanju Samson during the England series left him unable to sleep. Samson was named Player of the Tournament during India's T20 World Cup triumph earlier this year. India coach also used the episode to explain why even a player in exceptional form cannot automatically expect a place in India's playing XI.
